svg.title: The layers of @okikio/opfs
svg.desc: Your code calls FileSystemType. A bridge gives other libraries their own interface over it. FileSystemType calls one adapter, which has one of three shapes: file, object or record. The adapter calls a driver, the driver calls a client, and the client talks to the backend. One S3 write is traced through every layer.
svg.text: @okikio/opfs: one file API over every backend
Each layer answers one question. The orange path follows fs.writeFile("/notes/a.txt", bytes) to S3.
createFileSystem(adapter) → FileSystemType: one API, whatever the backend
read, write, stream, walk, copy, move, remove · plan() before I/O · locks between writers · metrics
stat().revision and writeFile(path, data, { ifRevision }) replace only the version you read
1. plan the write: size, mode, the backend's limits
A path becomes a key. Directories are
sync access and atomic rename where
One record per path; file bytes as
base64 data. Listing by parent path.
S3's limits. R2, GCS, Azure, B2 and
Deno, Bun and WebDAV have their own.
3. split into parts, keep the new ETag
S3, R2, GCS, Azure Blob, B2, Swift
A disk or the browser's OPFS
What stays out of each layer
· A client knows requests, not files.
· A driver knows one backend's rules, not file semantics.
· An adapter translates one shape into files; it does not re-implement the backend.
· A bridge adds no storage: it puts another library's interface on a FileSystemType you already have.
